title: Ghosts, history and a little mystery on the Georgetown Square

content:
I wouldn't necessarily consider myself a ghost hunter, but after spending an evening exploring the haunted history of downtown Georgetown with my husband and kids, I can certainly understand the appeal.

The Georgetown Ghost Tour, hosted by The Williamson Museum, offers a fascinating mix of local history, ghost stories and a little paranormal investigation, all set against the backdrop of Georgetown's historic downtown square.

And whether you're a firm believer in ghosts or someone who approaches the supernatural with a healthy dose of skepticism, I can confidently say it's an entertaining experience for both.

Our tour guide for the evening was Danelle Houck, executive director of The Williamson Museum, who proved to be just as entertaining as the stories she shared. Houck has a knack for storytelling, blending historical facts, humor and a little mystery in a way that kept our group engaged throughout the walking tour.

What I appreciated most was that the experience wasn't simply about trying to convince us that ghosts exist. Instead, it was an opportunity to learn about Georgetown's past through the stories of people who once lived, worked and walked the very streets we were exploring.

Of course, the possibility that some of those former residents might still be hanging around made things a little more interesting.

Throughout the tour, we learned about the ghosts that have reportedly been seen, heard and even felt in buildings around the square. Some stories were a little spooky, others were simply fascinating, but each offered a glimpse into Georgetown's history that I probably wouldn't have discovered otherwise.

There's something especially intriguing about standing outside a historic building, hearing about the people who once occupied it and wondering whether their stories really ended when they died.

For our kids, however, the highlight of the evening was undoubtedly the ghost hunting.

The tour included opportunities to experiment with paranormal investigation equipment, including dowsing rods, which are traditionally used to locate underground water but have also become popular among ghost hunters who believe they can be used to communicate with spirits.

Naturally, the kids were all about it.

They loved getting to try the equipment for themselves, and I think the possibility of actually making contact with a ghost made the experience that much more exciting.

Did we encounter anything supernatural? I'll leave that open to interpretation.

But I will say that watching the kids experiment with the equipment and eagerly participate in the ghost-hunting activities was one of my favorite parts of the evening.

What surprised me, though, was how much they also enjoyed learning the history behind the hauntings.

They were genuinely interested in the stories of the ghosts that have reportedly made appearances around the square, and the combination of history and mystery seemed to capture their attention in a way a traditional history lesson might not.

And really, that's what makes this tour so enjoyable.

You don't have to believe in ghosts to appreciate a good ghost story, especially when it's connected to the history of a place you know.

I've visited the Georgetown Square plenty of times but walking around it at night while listening to stories of its past gave me an entirely different perspective.

It's easy to admire the beautiful historic buildings, browse the shops or enjoy a meal downtown without giving much thought to the generations of people who came before us.

The ghost tour changes that.

Suddenly, those familiar buildings become places filled with stories, personalities and mysteries. Whether the reported paranormal encounters have a supernatural explanation or not, the history behind them is fascinating.

Houck did an excellent job of bringing those stories to life, and her enthusiasm for Georgetown's history was evident throughout the evening. She managed to make the tour educational without ever making it feel like a history lecture, which is no small accomplishment when you're leading a group of people around downtown after dark.

As far as family activities go, I would absolutely recommend the experience, with one small consideration.

While our kids thoroughly enjoyed the tour, I think it's best suited for children ages 10 and older. Younger kids might love the idea of hunting ghosts and experimenting with the equipment, but much of the experience involves walking, listening and learning about local history. For younger children, that might become a little tedious.

For older kids, teenagers and adults, though, it's a great combination of entertainment, education and just enough spooky fun.

I also appreciated that the experience didn't rely on jump scares or elaborate haunted-house theatrics. The stories themselves provided the entertainment, and the historic setting added plenty of atmosphere.

In fact, I think that's one of the best things about the Georgetown Ghost Tour. It appeals to a much wider audience than just paranormal enthusiasts.

History buffs will appreciate learning more about Georgetown's past. Ghost believers will enjoy hearing about the reported encounters and trying out the investigation equipment. Skeptics can have just as much fun listening to the stories and deciding for themselves what they believe.

And families like ours get to enjoy an evening doing something a little different together.

By the end of the tour, I can't say I was any closer to proving that ghosts exist, but I certainly walked away with a greater appreciation for Georgetown's history and a few stories I'll probably think about the next time I'm strolling around the square.

The Williamson Museum has found a creative and entertaining way to connect people with local history, and Houck's engaging storytelling makes the experience all the more memorable.

We went looking for ghosts, but we came away with something even better: a fun family memory and a new perspective on a place we thought we already knew.

And who knows? Maybe the next time we're walking around the Georgetown Square, we'll have a little more company than we realize.

For more information about the Georgetown Ghost Tours, visit williamsonmuseum.org.
